issues.legal_issue: A will relied on to defeat a claim of intestate succession must be proved in accordance with the statutory requirements for execution and attestation, and the scribe's signature alone does not satisfy those requirements unless the scribe signed with the intention to attest.
material_facts: The defendant relied on a will to defeat the plaintiffs’ claim to the property.
The scribe testified only that he wrote the will and did not say that he signed it to attest to the testator’s execution.
The scribe could not remember the names of the attesting witnesses.
issues.conclusion: The will was not duly proved and could not defeat the claim based on intestate succession.
issues.legal_principle: A will must be proved as required by Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 and Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, including by calling at least one attesting witness when the statutory conditions apply. A scribe is not an attesting witness merely by signing as the writer; the required intention to attest must be shown. The Court applied H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur, M.L. Abdul Jabbar Sahib v. M.V. Venkata Sastri & Sons, and N. Kamalam v. Ayyasamy.

predicates.will_based_title_defense: In a property-title proceeding, a party relied on a will to defeat another party’s claim to the property.
predicates.no_attesting_witness_examined: The party relying on the will did not call any attesting witness to prove its execution.
predicates.scribe_signed_only_as_writer: The person who wrote the will testified or appeared only as its writer and did not establish that they signed it intending to attest its execution.

issues.definition: When a party relies on a will in a property-title proceeding, and no attesting witness is examined and the writer signed only as a scribe, the will is not duly proved.

issues.legal_issue: A statement acknowledging that a will was made is not an admission of its genuine or duly executed character unless it clearly admits those matters.
material_facts: A pleading in a later suit referred to a will in favour of the beneficiary.
The witness said he learned about the will from the opposing party’s written statement and did not admit its genuineness.
The High Court treated the references as admissions that made independent proof unnecessary.
issues.conclusion: The statements did not admit the genuineness or due execution of the will and did not dispense with the need to prove it.
issues.legal_principle: A clear and true admission can be decisive and may dispense with proof, but a reference to the making of a will is not an admission of its genuineness or due execution. The Court applied Section 58 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and relied on Narayan Bhagwantrao Gosavi Balajiwale v. Gopal Vinayak Gosavi, Nagindas Ramdas v. Dalpatram Ichharam, and Gautam Sarup v. Leela Jetly.

predicates.will_based_title_defense: In a property-title proceeding, a party relied on a will to defeat another party’s claim to the property.
predicates.statements_only_acknowledge_will_made: The opposing party’s statements referred to the making or existence of a will without clearly accepting its legal validity.
predicates.no_clear_admission_of_genuine_execution: The opposing party did not clearly admit that the will was genuine and duly executed.

issues.definition: If the statements in a property-title proceeding acknowledge only that a will was made and do not clearly admit its genuine execution, the will still requires independent proof.

issues.legal_issue: A will surrounded by suspicious circumstances cannot be accepted unless its propounder removes the legitimate doubts raised by those circumstances.
material_facts: The will gave the property to one beneficiary while excluding the testator’s other daughters without a convincing reason.
The will did not identify the specific property bequeathed.
The beneficiary participated in the preparation and registration of the will and was present when it was executed and presented for registration.
The will was presented for registration on separate occasions, and the witnesses did not satisfactorily explain the circumstances.
The evidence did not explain how the will came into the propounder’s possession or establish its proper custody.
The propounder did not satisfactorily explain the circumstances identified by the first appellate court.
issues.conclusion: The suspicious circumstances were not removed, so the will could not be accepted as genuine.
issues.legal_principle: The propounder bears the initial burden of proving the will and, where suspicious circumstances surround its execution, must remove all legitimate doubts with cogent and convincing evidence. The burden is heavier in such cases, and mere assertions or registration do not by themselves remove suspicion. The Court applied H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur, and Ramachandra v. Champabia.

predicates.will_dispute: A party’s claim to property depended on whether a will was genuine.
predicates.will_surrounded_by_suspicious_circumstan: The circumstances of the will’s preparation, contents, beneficiaries, execution, registration, or custody gave reason to doubt its genuineness.
predicates.propounder_failed_to_remove_legitimate_d: The party relying on the will did not provide a cogent and convincing explanation that removed the legitimate doubts raised by the circumstances.

issues.definition: In a dispute over a will, if circumstances raise legitimate doubts and the propounder does not remove them with cogent and convincing evidence, the will is not accepted as genuine.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court reversing a first appellate court’s findings on a will must examine the material evidence and the reasons for those findings rather than dismissing them as conjectural without addressing the identified suspicious circumstances.
material_facts: The first appellate court gave reasons based on the evidence for finding the will unproved and surrounded by suspicious circumstances.
The High Court reversed that decision, relying on alleged admissions and describing the first appellate court’s findings as conjectural.
The High Court did not properly examine the evidence underlying the first appellate court’s findings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s reversal could not stand; the Supreme Court set it aside and restored the first appellate court’s judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Where the first appellate court has identified evidentiary grounds for finding a will unproved and suspicious, the reviewing court must carefully examine the relevant evidence and determine whether the propounder removed the legitimate suspicion. The Court applied the principles governing proof of wills in H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma and Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur.

predicates.second_appeal_reverses_first_appellate_w: A High Court in a second appeal reversed the first appellate court’s finding about whether a will was proved.
predicates.first_appellate_court_gave_evidence_base: The first appellate court supported its finding with reasons drawn from the evidence and identified circumstances surrounding the will.
predicates.high_court_failed_to_examine_relevant_ev: The High Court rejected those reasons without properly examining the material evidence on which they rested.

issues.definition: When a High Court reverses an evidence-based first appellate finding about a will without examining the relevant evidence, its reversal is set aside.
